Laya as a Typed Probabilistic Assessor:
An Independent Reproduction and a Preregistered Study of
Calibration and Selective Escalation

Gowthamkumar Nandakishore
September 2026
Abstract

The shipped Laya Typed-Decisions checkpoint, a 421M-parameter ModernBERT-large assessor that answers typed choice/noul/score questions over workflow state, is uniformly under-confident. The signed confidence–accuracy gap is −0.214-0.214, every occupied reliability bin’s accuracy exceeds its confidence, and that sign uniformity collapses every binned ECE variant to the same value, 0.2140.214. The card frames the risk as over-confidence; the measured direction is the opposite, and the direction decides which way a confidence-gated cascade fails. A single disjointly fitted temperature (T=0.469T{=}0.469, sharpening) removes most of the miscalibration (held-out ECE 0.204→0.0370.204\to 0.037) and outperforms the shipped per-option-count table. The frozen selection rule instead chose isotonic regression, which overfit and failed its held-out NLL contrast on both tracks, so hypothesis H2 is not supported. Re-running the released checkpoint on its full official test split reproduces the card’s headline accuracy (0.7670.767 vs. 0.7660.766). The retrospective E1 reproduction preceded the analysis freeze; E2–E8 were prospectively preregistered, and 20 of 22 executed confirmatory tests reject under Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q=0.05q{=}0.05 (two descoped). The frozen gate beats random escalation but misses its 10%10\% accepted-set error target on both tracks, an exploratory out-of-distribution probe finds no zero-shot transfer (accuracy 0.6170.617), and every score measures agreement with a synthetic teacher whose self-agreement ceiling (0.7350.735) the specialist exceeds. Per-decision predictions, run manifests, and the frozen preregistration are in the ancillary files. The author has no affiliation with the model’s publisher, the dataset’s publisher, or TypeSafe (§13).

Keywords: typed decisions; language-model evaluation; assessor; calibration; selective prediction; reproducibility; preregistration

1 Introduction

Automated assessment increasingly routes real decisions, such as whether an agent trace needs human review, whether an invoice is paid or held, and whether a security alert is closed or contained. A typed decision interface serves this setting directly. The model receives one piece of unstructured state and several typed questions, and returns a probability distribution over each question’s label space rather than free text. This differs from reference-based answer grading, where a candidate is compared with a supplied reference (Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026), and from general verification, where a solution or trajectory receives a graded quality score (Kwok et al., 2026). It is closest in interface to decision-only judging services (Li et al., 2026)11 1 Li et al. (2026) evaluate the commercial TypeSafe JEV service as a black box; that study is independent of TypeSafe and of this work., but the artifact studied here is small, open-weight, and local.

The gap this paper addresses is the distance between a reported benchmark accuracy and a deployable confidence signal. The public model card for Laya Typed-Decisions reports 0.7660.766 accuracy on its benchmark’s test split (reported, model card22 2 https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions, accessed 2026-09-26; revision 1a793eb5.). Yet the same card instructs users to treat the checkpoint’s confidence as uncalibrated, and its shipped temperature configuration is known to be misconfigured: the temperatures fitted during training used a slice of the training data (reported, model card), and they are overridden at inference by an inherited per-option-count table whose out-of-range choice:11+ entry is clamped by laya 0.3.20 (measured). Whether such an artifact can act as a trustworthy first-stage assessor (accepting decisions when confident and escalating when unsure, as Li et al. (2026) frame it for a proprietary hosted judge) is an empirical question that its card does not answer.

This is an independent study. The author has no affiliation with Convai Innovations, which publishes the model, its base model, and the laya package; with the LocalLLaMA organization, which publishes the benchmark; or with TypeSafe (§13). What the study supplies is a frozen protocol, frozen thresholds, and per-decision artifacts that let anyone check or extend the numbers. A previously circulated draft of this work was a protocol-only manuscript that proposed the evaluation and reported no measurements. This version executes that protocol in two registers. The reproduction (E1) ran first and is retrospective, predating the preregistration under the plan’s fit-nothing exemption. The plan was then frozen, and every prospectively frozen analysis (E2–E8) executed against the frozen thresholds; only those analyses are claimed as preregistered. §3.7 states the timing, including the acceptance-gate item it fails, and Appendix D gives the full execution timeline. The one descoped component is the external-validity set (E9; §9).

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    A decomposition of the card’s miscalibration (E4). The shipped checkpoint is uniformly under-confident (signed gap −0.214-0.214), not over-confident as the card’s guidance implies; one disjointly fitted temperature removes almost all of it (held-out ECE 0.204→0.0370.204\to 0.037), and the fitted temperature sharpens (T=0.47T{=}0.47) where the shipped override softens (T=1.25T{=}1.25–1.981.98). The inherited configuration is directionally backwards on this benchmark.

  2. 2.

    An escalation analysis with explicit scope limits (E5–E6). No runnable strong judge exists in this study’s environment (an author-directed constraint in the frozen plan), so cascade end-to-end accuracy is reported only as an oracle-escalation upper bound with the escalation target’s accuracy and cost as explicit symbolic parameters, alongside a random-escalation control at matched rate. The confidence signal does real work (E1t/E2t, +6.5+6.5/+7.6+7.6 accepted-set accuracy points over random escalation, both FDR-significant), yet the frozen gate misses its 10%10\% error target out-of-sample and passes confidently wrong security decisions (§7). The proprietary JEV service is never run (no API access exists) and appears only as third-party context with its source’s own disclaimer.

  3. 3.

    A preregistered analysis protocol, frozen after the reproduction and before all fitting. All thresholds, temperature-fitting procedures, split assignments, confidence statistics, hypothesis operationalizations, and a 24-test false-discovery-rate family were frozen (2026-09-26, 15:50 UTC) before any fitting touched the test split, and the frozen choices were then followed even where they hurt; the frozen method-selection rule picked an overfit calibrator on both tracks (§6). The design separates a split-half protocol on the released checkpoint (Track A) from a clean re-training replication (Track B), because the released checkpoint’s calibration data is contaminated by construction (§3.3).

  4. 4.

    An independent reproduction of the released checkpoint (E1). We re-run it on all 400 test cases and report every headline metric against the card’s reported values with 95% BCa confidence intervals from a case-level cluster bootstrap (the 2,000 decisions are five-per-case and correlated; decision-level intervals would be too narrow, Appendix E). Soft accuracy is the one headline metric that fails to reproduce (0.5090.509 vs. 0.4710.471; CI excludes the reported value) and is recorded as an open reproducibility finding (§4). We release the per-decision prediction artifact (2,000 rows); the model card publishes no per-decision record behind its headline numbers. Per-decision artifacts for every headline run are released as well.

  5. 5.

    A clean replication that prices contamination (Track B). Re-training from the pinned base with the card’s recipe, on case-level splits, on one Apple-silicon device, reproduces test accuracy within noise (0.7710.771 vs. 0.7670.767; paired p=0.57p{=}0.57). Its cleanly calibrated identity configuration already has ECE 0.1510.151 vs. the released 0.2140.214, while a probe that refits temperatures on trained-on items degrades held-out ECE 3.7×3.7\times (0.024→0.0870.024\to 0.087), a direct measurement of what the card’s contaminated calibration protocol costs (§8).

2 Related work

Reference-based encoder assessment.

Gisserot-Boukhlef et al. (2026) show across 36 models and 15 tasks that lexical answer matching correlates poorly with human judgment, and train an encoder (EuroBERT-210M; Boizard et al., 2025) on question–candidate–reference triplets to judge correctness in reference-based settings. Two of their findings frame our study. Their encoder’s soft probabilities are usably calibrated after a single temperature (τ=1.75\tau{=}1.75). And their cost-effective fallback cascade, regex grading first with the encoder only where regex fails, cuts total compute roughly 5×5\times when regex fails on 20% of items (third-party; their benchmarks). Laya Typed-Decisions descends from the same encoder lineage (it is a ModernBERT-large checkpoint; Warner et al., 2024), but its task is not reference-based; the benchmark supplies no reference answers, so BERT-as-a-Judge is not runnable here and none of its numbers can be compared to ours (preregistration §0.2).

Confidence-gated cascades.

Selective prediction descends from the reject option (Chow, 1970) through selective deep networks (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017). For language models, FrugalGPT sequences cheaper models before expensive ones (Chen et al., 2024), and Jitkrittum et al. (2023) characterize when confidence-based deferral is sufficient in principle. Closest to us, JEV-as-a-Judge (Li et al., 2026) studies a decision-only judge whose maximum label probability gates escalation to a stronger generative judge. Their frozen cascade at threshold 0.90.9 accepts 53.7%53.7\% of items and retains ∼99%{\sim}99\% of the strong judge’s accuracy at ∼57{\sim}57–62%62\% of its fee (third-party; their benchmarks). Three facts matter for reading this paper against theirs. JEV is a proprietary hosted service evaluated as a black box; its benchmarks are five public judge suites, none of them the four workflow domains studied here; and its authors have never evaluated it on those domains. We run nothing against JEV (no API access exists; the frozen plan forbids any JEV run or estimate) and make no head-to-head claim.

Fine-grained verification.

LLM-as-a-Verifier (Kwok et al., 2026) computes continuous quality scores as expectations over scoring-token logits and scales verification along granularity, repetition, and criteria decomposition, reporting state-of-the-art results on agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench V2 86.5%86.5\%, SWE-Bench Verified 78.2%78.2\%, RoboRewardBench 87.4%87.4\%, MedAgentBench 73.3%73.3\%; third-party). Laya’s interface is materially different (a trained encoder emitting distributions over typed label spaces rather than scoring-token readout from a generative model), but the shared lesson is that probability shape beyond the argmax carries the operational signal.

Calibration and selective prediction measurement.

Modern networks are often miscalibrated and temperature scaling is the standard post-hoc remedy (Guo et al., 2017). Binned ECE is a biased estimator; bin placement changes the number (Nixon et al., 2019; Roelofs et al., 2022), and recalibrated models can be less calibrated than they report (Kumar et al., 2019). We therefore report an ECE family (equal-width at several bin counts, equal-mass, classwise, and a signed confidence–accuracy gap) with proper scoring rules (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007) rather than a single ECE. Judge-style evaluators also carry presentation biases, in particular position and order sensitivity (Zheng et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024), which motivates the frozen robustness suite (E7). On statistics, we follow bootstrap practice for clustered data (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993; Davison and Hinkley, 1997), Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), and preregistration norms (Nosek et al., 2018).

3 Setup

3.1 Model

Laya Typed-Decisions is a 421M-parameter typed-decision checkpoint built on ModernBERT-large (Warner et al., 2024), released by Convai Innovations (footnote 2). It answers three primitives: choice (distribution over NN labels), noul (probability a statement is true), and score (distribution over ordered rubric levels plus an expected score). Per its card (reported), it was fine-tuned from the convaiinnovations/laya base with an RLCD-style recipe: the policy emits a distribution over typed options, and exploration adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to logits (σ\sigma annealed →0.10.4\!\to\!0.1). The reward is a strictly proper scoring rule (log plus 0.75⋅0.75\cdotspherical, plus a ranked probability score term for ordinal score questions); updates are REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline plus soft cross-entropy against teacher distributions. At inference the shipped configuration applies a per-option-count temperature table (choice:3-5 =1.760=1.760, noul:2 =1.983=1.983, score:3-5 =1.251=1.251, …; measured, read from the pinned checkpoint) which overrides per-type temperatures fitted during training, temperatures that were themselves fitted on a slice of the training data (reported, model card). The card’s own instruction is to treat shipped confidence as uncalibrated. We evaluate the checkpoint exactly as shipped, bug and all, through laya 0.3.20 predict_batch.

3.2 Benchmark and the teacher-label caveat

The Typed Decisions benchmark33 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions, accessed 2026-09-26; revision f7a2487e. The dataset is independent of, and unaffiliated with, TypeSafe. The LocalLLaMA organization on Hugging Face that publishes it is distinct from the Reddit community of the same name. has four workflow subsets (agent_trace_observability, customer_service, invoice_processing, security_incidents), each with 300 train and 100 test cases; every case asks five typed questions over one shared state, giving 6,000 train and 2,000 test decisions. Option criteria descriptions are part of the input. Gold labels are the mean of three samples from a teacher endpoint (roughly 4B-class capability, temperature 0.7; reported, dataset card); a label_agreement field records how much the samples disagreed.

Three dataset-card reference points (reported) anchor interpretation: a majority baseline scores 0.5200.520 (on the combined 1,600 cases), a model with perfect knowledge of the latent generating factors scores 0.7040.704, and teacher self-agreement, a fresh teacher sample scored against gold built from the others, scores 0.7350.735. The card’s own reading is that “a score much above 0.75 means a model has learned the teacher’s quirks rather than the task.” Agreement with a teacher is not correctness (Gudibande et al., 2023); the dataset card gives a concrete example where the teacher missed a duplicate invoice. Every number in this paper measures teacher agreement on synthetic cases, and §10 returns to what that does and does not support. The card also separates specialist models (fitted on these four workflows) from generalist ones (zero-shot on unseen schemas) and warns the two are not comparable rows; we preserve that grouping everywhere.

3.3 Split design (Track A and Track B)

The released checkpoint was fine-tuned on all 1,200 training cases, so any temperature or threshold fitted on training data is contaminated, the defect its card admits. The frozen design therefore runs two tracks and reports both.

Track A (split-half test protocol; released checkpoint). The 400 official test cases are partitioned at case level, stratified by workflow (50/50 per workflow), into calib (200 cases, 1,000 decisions) and eval (200 cases, 1,000 decisions), with generator and seed fixed in the preregistration (NumPy PCG64, seed 20260926; ID lists in track_a_split.json, SHA-256 7719b147…). Every temperature and threshold is fitted on calib only; all Track A headline results are reported on eval only. eval results are not directly comparable to the card’s 2,000-decision figures (half the sample); the full-400 reproduction (E1) is reported separately and labeled as such, not as a calibrated result.

Track B (clean replication). We fine-tune our own specialist from the pinned laya base model with the card’s RLCD recipe (§3.1), splitting the 1,200 training cases at case level into 960 fine-tune / 240 validation (stratified, seed 20260926). Calibration and cascade thresholds are fitted only on the 240 validation cases; the 400-case test split is evaluated exactly once. Track A answers whether the released artifact can be used responsibly today; Track B answers whether the method works when the protocol is clean. Hypotheses H2/H3 are primarily tested on Track B.

3.4 Comparators

The preregistration (its §0, an author-directed amendment recorded before the freeze) restricts execution to models runnable on the local machine. The frozen measured comparator set:

  • •

    Laya Typed-Decisions, released (Track A);

  • •

    our Track B replication;

  • •

    the laya base checkpoint zero-shot under the same question contract (card reports 0.3620.362; reported, to verify);

  • •

    laya-multilingual (mmBERT-base, 322M; its card notes no fitted temperatures at all);

  • •

    a ModernBERT-base specialist trained by us with the Track B recipe (the dataset card lists its own frozen-encoder specialist at 0.6460.646; reported);

  • •

    trivial baselines: majority class per question, uniform, training-set prior (model card reports majority 0.4610.461 and random 0.3180.318; dataset card reports uniform 0.3080.308 and prior 0.4700.470 on its own scoring; all reported);

  • •

    the teacher self-agreement ceiling, recomputed from the dataset’s three-sample fields (card reports 0.7350.735; reported).

The same directive dropped any API generative judge and any local ∼{\sim}8B generative judge. Consequently no runnable escalation target exists, with the consequences for E5/E6 spelled out in §7. Comparators are grouped by task access and training exposure in every table; a workflow specialist and a zero-shot generalist are never ranked as interchangeable rows.

JEV, third-party only. The dataset card’s maintainers measured TypeSafe JEV 1.13.0 through its public API on 2026-09-18 (all 400 test cases): accuracy 0.7270.727, soft accuracy 0.5800.580, Brier 0.1480.148, ECE 0.1440.144 (signed over-confidence +0.023+0.023), score MAE 0.3910.391, p50 latency 710 ms/case, end-to-end through the public API, one request at a time (third-party; footnote 3). This is the only JEV latency figure verifiable at the pinned dataset-card revision; it is quoted with that measurement’s own scope and makes no intrinsic inference-time claim. The Laya model card quotes JEV comparison figures with an explicit disclaimer, which we adopt: these numbers were not measured in this work; prompts, pipeline, and sample handling differ; no superiority claim in either direction is made from them. JEV nearly saturates this benchmark (0.7270.727 against the teacher self-agreement ceiling, per the dataset card), which further limits what any comparison could show. The same card, at the pinned revision, also lists a hosted zero-shot model, meraGPT Decider 1, at 0.7680.768 accuracy, Brier 0.0520.052, and score MAE 0.2190.219 (third-party; the card’s own measurement dated 2026-09-22), above both JEV and the teacher self-agreement ceiling. It is not run here (no API access) and appears only as third-party context under the same disclaimer.

3.5 Metrics

All metric definitions are frozen in code (metrics.py; the metric code and its unit tests are in the ancillary files). The 42 unit tests comprise 41 against hand-computed cases plus one cross-check against the shipped laya.common.ece_score; 36 existed at the freeze and six were added with the ECEsweep\mathrm{ECE}_{\mathrm{sweep}} implementation under deviation D1. Metric definitions are pinned to laya/common.py in the laya 0.3.20 PyPI package and to the card’s published evaluation conventions. For decision ii with predicted distribution pp and teacher distribution gg over KK options:

  • •

    Accuracy: 𝟏[argmaxkpk=argmaxkgk]\mathbf{1}[\arg\max_{k}p_{k}=\arg\max_{k}g_{k}], averaged over decisions; gold argmax follows the teacher-majority rule of the fine-tuning notebook linked from the model card (footnote 2), “the notebook” hereafter.

  • •

    Macro-F1: per-class F1=2​TP/(2​TP+FP+FN)F_{1}=2\,\mathrm{TP}/(2\,\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}) over option positions, unweighted mean.

  • •

    Soft accuracy: ∑kpk​gk\sum_{k}p_{k}g_{k} after the notebook’s 10−610^{-6} missing-key floor and renormalization, averaged over choice and noul decisions only (n=1,200n{=}1{,}200 of 2,000); the notebook’s score arm never contributes. This scope is extracted from the card’s own code; the card’s 0.4710.471 is this quantity.

  • •

    Brier: ∑k(pk−yk)2\sum_{k}(p_{k}-y_{k})^{2} averaged over decisions. The card’s 0.0620.062 takes yy to be the teacher’s soft distribution and averages over choice+noul only (verified against the notebook’s code); we compute both this form and the one-hot-gold form. The frozen plan misattributed the card’s figure to the one-hot form; deviation D6 (Appendix C) records the correction, which changes no measured value.

  • •

    NLL: −mean⁡log⁡max⁡(pgold,10−12)-\operatorname{mean}\log\max(p_{\text{gold}},10^{-12}).

  • •

    RPS (ordinal score questions): ∑k(CDFp​(k)−CDFy​(k))2/(K−1)\sum_{k}(\mathrm{CDF}_{p}(k)-\mathrm{CDF}_{y}(k))^{2}/(K-1), matching the training reward’s form.

  • •

    ECE family: the card’s convention as frozen (10 equal-width bins; first bin closed at the bottom, others (lo,hi](\mathrm{lo},\mathrm{hi}]; empty bins skipped; mass-weighted) for card comparability. Also equal-width with M∈{10,15,20}M\in\{10,15,20\}, of which M=15M{=}15 is the frozen confirmatory endpoint (a draft mislabeling is reconciled as deviation D7, Appendix C, with no numeric effect); equal-mass (adaptive) binning (Nixon et al., 2019); and classwise calibration error over option positions. The signed gap == mean confidence −- accuracy shows the direction ECE hides. ECEsweep\mathrm{ECE}_{\mathrm{sweep}} (Roelofs et al., 2022) is in the frozen family; its unit-tested implementation landed slightly after the E4 calib extraction began (deviation D1, Appendix C) and it is reported wherever the ECE family appears.

  • •

    Error-detection AUROC/AUPRC: errors as the positive class, score −q-q where q=maxk⁡pkq=\max_{k}p_{k}; plus AURC for selective prediction.

The frozen confidence statistic is q=maxk⁡pkq=\max_{k}p_{k} of the post-calibration distribution; entropy, margin, and ordinal variance are secondary ablations only.

3.6 Uncertainty quantification and multiplicity

The 2,000 test decisions sit in 400 case clusters (five decisions per case, same document and context), so decisions are not independent. Every confidence interval in this paper is a case-level cluster bootstrap: resample cases with replacement, keep each case’s five decisions together, nboot=10,000n_{\mathrm{boot}}=10{,}000, seed 0; BCa intervals primary for single-quantity metrics, percentile as robustness check (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993; Davison and Hinkley, 1997). Model comparisons use paired differences on identical resampled case sets; paired-difference intervals are percentile (BCa on a difference needs a combined jackknife and was not preregistered for the paired case). Bootstrap p-values use the finite-sample add-one convention (b+1)/(B+1)(b{+}1)/(B{+}1), doubled for two-sided tests, so zero exceedances in B=10,000B{=}10{,}000 resamples is reported as p≤10−4p\leq 10^{-4} (one-sided) or p≤2×10−4p\leq 2{\times}10^{-4} (two-sided), the resolution limit instead of zero. Naive i.i.d. decision-level intervals appear only in a frozen appendix contrast (Figure 8). Confirmatory inference is limited to a frozen family of 24 tests with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control at q=0.05q=0.05 (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995); everything else is exploratory and labeled as such. Under the preregistration’s §0.a scope amendment, the two external-validity family members (F1t/F2t) could not execute in this version and are reported as not executed; the BH denominator conservatively remains the full family size of 24 (equivalent to assigning them p=1p{=}1). Twenty of the 22 executed tests reject (Appendix E).

3.7 Preregistration and test-set exposure

The analysis plan was frozen on 2026-09-26 at 15:50 UTC, before any fitting touched the test split (Nosek et al., 2018); the frozen document is released verbatim as an ancillary file and its SHA-256 is listed in anc/README.txt. Timestamps are taken from the run manifests, which are also released. The freeze time itself is the author’s own statement; the frozen document dates its own authorization to 21:16 IST (15:46 UTC) on 2026-09-26, and the first post-freeze manifest is timestamped 15:51:06 UTC, which brackets it. E1 predates the freeze. The preregistration (its §2) quotes the plan clause that exempts the reproduction because it fits nothing (no temperature, threshold, prompt, or model choice was informed by test labels). But the same plan’s higher-priority integrity rule, that the official test split is opened only after all choices are frozen, and its acceptance-gate wording (preregistration frozen before the first test evaluation) admit no exemption. The two plan clauses conflict; the conflict was resolved in favor of running E1 first, so E1 and H1 are retrospective, only E2–E8 are prospectively preregistered, and the acceptance gate’s timing item is recorded as a disclosed failure in gate.json. Post-freeze test-set exposure, exhaustively:

  • •

    one accidental partial smoke re-run of the exempt E1 pipeline (logged; Appendix C);

  • •

    the calib fitting pass (E4);

  • •

    two failed E4 attempts at 16:05:29 and 16:05:59 UTC (Python exceptions; manifested; read calib cases before failing);

  • •

    the single frozen eval pass (E5–E6);

  • •

    Track B’s single 400-case test pass;

  • •

    one full-400 pass per frozen comparator (each exactly once, manifested);

  • •

    E7’s perturbation forwards, which run on calib cases only;

  • •

    the 2026-09-27 fp32/CPU rerun of all 400 test cases (fits nothing; deviation D10, Appendix C);

  • •

    the 2026-09-27 version-bisection reruns of all 400 test cases, one per evaluated laya release (0.3.3 and 0.3.20), plus one single-case API schema check under 0.3.3 (all fit nothing; deviation D11).

E8 consumes only records stored by the single eval pass; no new eval forwards occurred after step 8. Hypothesis H1’s numerical criterion (|Δ|≤0.02|\Delta|\leq 0.02) was articulated after E1 ran and is therefore a post-hoc reporting structure for E1 rather than a preregistered prediction; H2–H4 and all thresholds were frozen before any calib/eval or Track B access. Every raw-logit extraction used by E4/E5 was cross-checked against the E1 predict_batch predictions (2,000/2,000 decisions, max probability difference 1.2×10−41.2\times 10^{-4}, within the stored files’ 4-decimal rounding).

4 Reproduction of the released checkpoint (E1)

E1 runs the released checkpoint, as shipped (including the inherited temperature_by_options override), on all 400 test cases / 2,000 decisions: laya 0.3.20 predict_batch, one case per call, max sequence length 1024, batch size 1, Apple M5 Max (64 GB, mps), Python 3.12.14, torch 2.14.0, transformers 5.17.0. Every number labeled measured below comes from the logged, manifested run whose artifacts are released in the ancillary files; reported numbers are transcribed from the model card (footnote 2). Nothing was tuned toward the reported values.

4.1 Headline metrics match the card, except soft accuracy

Accuracy, Brier, ECE, score MAE, all four per-workflow accuracies, and all six per-primitive statistics reproduce the card within +0.004+0.004 (Tables 1–2); the argmax pipeline therefore matches the card’s, and H1 is supported on those metrics under the (post-hoc, §3.7) |Δ|≤0.02|\Delta|\leq 0.02 criterion. Candidate failure causes named in the frozen plan for investigation (tokenizer version, batch-size padding effects, option-count clamping) were not pursued further for these metrics because the deltas were trivial.

Open reproducibility finding 1, narrowed twice: soft accuracy does not reproduce; precision, backend, and the released harness range are ruled out.

Measured 0.50860.5086 [0.4987,0.5196][0.4987,0.5196] against a reported 0.4710.471. The interval excludes the reported value, so this is a pipeline difference rather than sampling noise. Because accuracy, ECE, and Brier all reproduce closely, the predicted distributions must be close to the card’s; a distribution slightly more concentrated on the teacher’s mode raises ∑kpk​gk\sum_{k}p_{k}g_{k} while barely moving ∑k(pk−gk)2\sum_{k}(p_{k}-g_{k})^{2} or max-probability calibration. Two exploratory reruns of the same 2,000 decisions narrow the cause. An fp32/CPU rerun (deviation D10; artifact e1_fp32_cpu_probe.json) reproduces the canonical run (F16 weights under bf16 autocast on MPS) almost exactly (soft accuracy 0.50870.5087; maximum per-decision probability difference 0.00790.0079; 4 argmax flips of 2,000), ruling out numeric precision and the MPS backend. A version bisection of the laya inference harness then reran the decisions in one fresh virtual environment per release (deviation D11; artifacts e1_version_probe_*.json). Torch and transformers were pinned to the canonical versions in every environment. laya 0.3.20 reproduces the canonical run byte-identically at the stored 4-decimal rounding (maximum probability difference 0.00.0). laya 0.3.3, the lower endpoint of the planned bisection range (released 2026-09-19, single-state predict API), measures soft accuracy 0.50870.5087. The two endpoints agree, so under the pre-stated rule no intermediate release was bisected: every released harness version from 0.3.3 to 0.3.20 is ruled out. What remains is the card-side pipeline itself (its exact package pins are not recoverable from the card): either its unreleased or pre-0.3.3-era evaluation code or a different data state produced 0.4710.471. The finding stays open, narrowed to the card side, with the per-decision files released so the card’s maintainers can close it.

4.2 The shipped checkpoint is under-confident, not over-confident

The signed calibration gap is −0.2142-0.2142 (measured), mean confidence 0.5530.553 against accuracy 0.7670.767. Figure 1 shows that every occupied reliability bin, in every primitive, sits above the diagonal (per-bin gaps −0.065-0.065 to −0.275-0.275 over 1,767 distinct confidence values). This explains an otherwise puzzling measurement. The entire binned-ECE family collapses to a single value, 0.214230.21423, for equal-width binning at M∈{10,15,20}M\in\{10,15,20\} and equal-mass binning (measured); when every bin’s gap has the same sign, mass-weighted binned ECE reduces to |mean confidence−accuracy||\text{mean confidence}-\text{accuracy}| regardless of binning scheme, a known failure mode of reading a single binned ECE (Nixon et al., 2019; Roelofs et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2019).

The direction also contradicts the card’s framing. The card instructs users to treat the checkpoint’s confidence as uncalibrated (guidance written around its known temperature-configuration defect), and its comparison table reads as an over-confidence concern; the dataset card separately reports JEV’s signed gap as over-confident (+0.023+0.023; third-party). The shipped Laya checkpoint measured here errs in the opposite direction. The inherited override applies only softening temperatures on this benchmark (all used buckets >1>1: 1.7601.760, 1.9831.983, 1.2511.251; measured), which divide the logits and depress qq uniformly. The magnitude of the card’s ECE (0.2130.213) is real, but its sign, on the shipped artifact, is under-confidence. Whether the raw pre-temperature logits are over-confident, i.e. how much of it is configuration artifact versus model, is the frozen E4 question (§6). For cascade deployment the direction matters. Uniform under-confidence inflates escalation rates (costly) rather than concealing errors (unsafe); the measured operating consequences appear in §7.

4.3 The temperature clamp is a no-op on this benchmark

The shipped override contains one out-of-range entry (choice:11+ =0.1006=0.1006, which laya 0.3.20 clamps to 0.50.5; measured). No test-split choice question has more than 5 options, so that bucket is never selected, and every bucket that is used is inside the clamp range (measured; clamp changes no used bucket). Running through predict_batch therefore reproduces the raw shipped configuration exactly here; the well-known choice:11+ sharpening bug does not drive the card’s headline ECE, and would only bite deployments with >>10-option questions.

4.4 Supplementary measured statistics and latency

On the full split (measured, exploratory): NLL 0.70690.7069 (ϵ=10−12\epsilon=10^{-12}); macro-F1 0.74990.7499; RPS on score questions 0.07950.0795 against one-hot gold and 0.01560.0156 against the teacher distribution; error-detection AUROC 0.75840.7584 and AUPRC 0.44230.4423 (errors positive, score −q-q). For context only, Li et al. (2026) report JEV error-detection AUROC of 0.869/0.745/0.8630.869/0.745/0.863 on their three benchmarks and near-chance 0.5180.518 on reference-free prose (third-party; different tasks, so no comparison is drawn). Whether 0.7580.758 is enough ranking signal for a useful cascade here is measured in §7.

Latency (measured, this hardware; the card’s T4 figures are on different hardware): batch size 1, first 3 cases discarded as warm-up; per-case p50/p90/p99 =95.9/124.1/195.4=95.9/124.1/195.4 ms (five decisions per case; p50 per decision 19.219.2 ms; 54.354.3 decisions/s). A batched throughput sweep measured 51.9/42.9/37.8/38.751.9/42.9/37.8/38.7 decisions/s at batch sizes 1/8/32/641/8/32/64; batching does not improve throughput on this MPS path (an unexplained, hardware-specific observation reported as-is; the card’s T4 claim of 103–332 questions/s batched is reported and untested here).

4.5 Released artifact

E1’s per-decision predictions are released as released_full_test.jsonl (2,000 rows; schema in Appendix B); the model card publishes no per-decision record behind its headline numbers, so this artifact makes the card’s headline independently re-analyzable, including every analysis in this paper, without model access. Canonical copies of all E1 artifacts are in the ancillary files.

5 Accuracy and probability quality across comparators (E2–E3)

All comparators of §3.4 were scored on the full 400-case test split, each exactly once, each with a run manifest; Table 3 groups them by task access and training exposure, per the dataset card’s own discipline. Trivial baselines are fitted on the 1,200 training cases only. Figure 2 shows the per-workflow reproduction with clustered intervals.

The zero-shot generalists confirm their cards (all measured). The laya base measures 0.36300.3630 against a reported 0.3620.362, and laya-multilingual (0.34950.3495), which ships no fitted temperatures at all, has the worst calibration in the table (ECE 0.3160.316); it sits below the majority baseline on accuracy, consistent with these schemas being unseen. The trivial baselines measure within 0.0230.023 of their card values (majority 0.48350.4835 vs. reported 0.4610.461 and prior 0.47850.4785 vs. 0.4700.470, both slightly above; uniform 0.31750.3175 vs. random 0.3180.318, slightly below). The first two plausibly differ by fitting split and tie-breaking convention, and are reported as our own measured definitions (majority/prior per (workflow, question) over training gold). The specialist–teacher gap is the dominant structure. Both large-encoder specialists sit at the teacher’s own self-agreement region, at least 0.280.28 above the strongest non-specialist row (majority, 0.48350.4835) and up to 0.450.45 above the weakest (uniform, 0.31750.3175). The interesting differences among them are in probability quality (NLL, ECE) rather than accuracy, which is where the released checkpoint’s inherited configuration hurts it (Track B’s clean identity beats it by 0.0800.080 NLL and 0.0630.063 ECE at indistinguishable accuracy; §8).

The RLCD recipe on a ModernBERT-base encoder does not reach the dataset card’s specialist row.

Our ModernBERT-base specialist, trained with the same RLCD recipe, splits, and epoch budget as Track B and differing only in the encoder, measures 0.54250.5425 [0.5145,0.5685][0.5145,0.5685], below the 0.6460.646 the dataset card reports (reported) for its ModernBERT-base specialist; the interval excludes the reported value. The two rows are not the same experiment. The card’s row is a frozen-encoder Adaptive Classifier (one classifier per question, mean pooling, 30 epochs; configuration published on the card and tuned on a held-out quarter of the training split), while ours fine-tunes the full encoder with the RLCD recipe. The gap therefore measures a training-method difference on a 149M-parameter encoder, and no reproducibility conclusion is drawn from it (Limitations, item 11). Under matched training the run still measures the encoder-capacity gap cleanly, 0.230.23 accuracy (paired Δ=−0.2245\Delta=-0.2245, p≤2×10−4p\leq 2{\times}10^{-4}) between ModernBERT-base and the large-encoder specialists.

E3’s interval discipline matters at this sample size. The case-cluster BCa interval on eval winner accuracy is ∼1.19×{\sim}1.19\times wider than the naive i.i.d. decision-level interval (measured; Figure 8, Appendix E); decision-level resampling would have overstated precision throughout.

6 Calibration (E4)

Six pre-specified methods were fitted on Track A calib (200 cases, 1,000 decisions; and independently on Track B’s 240-case validation split), never on eval or Track B test. The six methods:

  1. 1.

    identity, the shipped configuration including the inherited override, exactly as executed by laya 0.3.20;

  2. 2.

    single temperature;

  3. 3.

    per-primitive temperature (three parameters);

  4. 4.

    per-option-count temperature (the shipped configuration’s own parameterization, refitted properly);

  5. 5.

    vector scaling on the choice head;

  6. 6.

    isotonic regression (per-(primitive, position), one-vs-rest, renormalized).

Temperatures minimize NLL on the fitting split; the frozen selection rule picks the method with lowest fitting-split NLL. Table 4 reports both splits; Figure 1 (§4) shows the identity reliability diagrams this section repairs.

Most of the card’s miscalibration is removable by one disjointly fitted scalar, and the shipped override is directionally backwards.

One disjointly fitted scalar takes held-out ECE15 from 0.20350.2035 to 0.03720.0372 and NLL from 0.70270.7027 to 0.53640.5364 (A2/B2: Δ\DeltaNLL −0.166-0.166 [−0.198,−0.131][-0.198,-0.131], Δ\DeltaECE −0.166-0.166 [−0.191,−0.107][-0.191,-0.107], both p≤2×10−4p\leq 2{\times}10^{-4}, FDR-significant). The fitted temperature is T=0.469<1T=0.469<1; the logits need sharpening. The shipped configuration divides logits by T∈[1.25,1.98]T\in[1.25,1.98], softening, which is the wrong direction on this benchmark and mechanically explains the direction §4.2 measured. Per-primitive temperatures (0.410.41–0.540.54) buy almost nothing over the single scalar (Δ\DeltaNLL −0.0012-0.0012 on eval), and the per-option-count parameterization, the shipped configuration’s own functional form, is identical to per-primitive here because the benchmark’s fixed schemas occupy one option-count bucket per primitive. The shipped six-entry temperature table (of twelve possible buckets), including the clamped choice:11+ entry, cannot even be exercised by the benchmark that motivated it.

The frozen selection rule picked an overfit calibrator, on both tracks.

The frozen rule (lowest fitting-split NLL) selected isotonic regression, whose 66–2828 interpolation knots per (primitive, position) curve (median 21) won calib NLL by a wide margin (0.4460.446 vs. 0.5200.520) and then failed to transfer. Held-out NLL is 0.77380.7738, above identity, with a CI spanning [0.626,1.030][0.626,1.030] (the instability signature of near-zero fitted probabilities meeting held-out one-hot targets). Its confirmatory NLL contrast A6 does not reject (Δ=+0.071\Delta=+0.071 [−0.087,+0.263][-0.087,+0.263], p=0.446p=0.446), one of only two failures in the 22-test executed family. The same rule picked isotonic on Track B’s independent validation split and its NLL contrast failed there too (C6, p=0.108p=0.108; §8), so this is a replicated property of the selection rule at n=200n=200–240240 fitting cases rather than one unlucky split. Because H2 was operationalized as “the selected method improves held-out NLL and ECE,” H2 is formally not supported on either track, even though every temperature-family method (A2–A5, B2–B5, C2–C5, D2–D5) rejects decisively and isotonic’s own ECE contrast (B6/D6) rejects as well. The hypothesis failed under its frozen operationalization. A selection-by-NLL rule at this sample size prefers expressive monotone fits that do not generalize in NLL. We do not substitute a post-hoc winner; all downstream frozen analyses (E5) use isotonic as selected.

This also answers §4.2; the residual miscalibration after one scalar is ∼0.02{\sim}0.02–0.040.04 ECE, an operational statement about repairability rather than a unique model-versus-configuration decomposition. The error-detection AUROC moves only from 0.7660.766 (identity) to 0.7800.780 (single temperature) on eval; calibration reshapes confidence values but barely changes their ranking, which is what §7 gates on.

7 Selective escalation (E5) and cost (E6)

Protocol as frozen (preregistration §0/§5). Confidence is q=maxk⁡pkq=\max_{k}p_{k} after the selected calibration (isotonic, as selected; §6). Gating accepts a decision when q≥τq\geq\tau; τ∗\tau^{*} was chosen on calib from the frozen twelve-point grid as the smallest value with accepted-set error ≤0.10\leq 0.10, then frozen before the single eval pass. On calib this gave τdec∗=0.70\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{dec}}=0.70 (coverage 0.6440.644, accepted error 0.09160.0916) and τcase∗=0.80\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{case}}=0.80 (a case escalates if any of its five decisions falls below τ\tau; coverage on calib already only 0.0500.050). Because no runnable escalation target exists in this study (§3.4), end-to-end accuracy is reported only as the symbolic form c⋅a+(1−c)​aTc\cdot a+(1-c)\,a_{T} and its oracle bound (aT=1a_{T}=1); E6 cost likewise as cL+(1−c)​cTc_{L}+(1-c)\,c_{T} with cTc_{T} symbolic.

Operating point on eval (all measured, single frozen pass, 200 cases / 1,000 decisions).

Decision-level gating at τ∗=0.70\tau^{*}=0.70: coverage 0.6720.672 [0.637,0.704][0.637,0.704], accepted-set accuracy 0.86010.8601 [0.831,0.886][0.831,0.886], oracle-bounded end-to-end accuracy 0.9060.906 [0.885,0.923][0.885,0.923], escalation rate 0.3280.328. The frozen gate misses its target out-of-sample. Accepted-set error is 0.13990.1399 against the frozen 0.100.10; the calib-feasible threshold did not transfer (0.0916→0.13990.0916\to 0.1399), a 53%53\% relative degradation. H3(a) therefore fails on Track A (and, independently, on Track B: 0.0866→0.10280.0866\to 0.1028; §8). H3(b), that the confidence signal beats random escalation at matched rate, holds decisively: E1t Δ=+0.0646\Delta=+0.0646 [0.0502,0.0785][0.0502,0.0785], one-sided p≤10−4p\leq 10^{-4}, FDR-significant. So the signal is real but the frozen threshold’s error guarantee is not; a deployment would need to re-validate τ\tau on fresh data rather than trust a 200-case fit. Accuracy at fixed coverage (winner confidence ranking): 0.8000.800 at 90%90\%, 0.8390.839 at 75%75\%, 0.9080.908 at 50%50\%, 0.9760.976 at 25%25\%, from 0.7640.764 at full coverage; AURC 0.09930.0993 (winner) vs. 0.09960.0996 (identity), consistent with §6; calibration barely changes the ranking.

Why the frozen gate missed (exploratory, post hoc).

A decomposition of the stored per-decision records (deviation D9, Appendix C; artifact e11_tau_decomposition.json) shows the miss was built in at fitting time. Under the identity ranking, which no calibration map fitted on calib can change, accepted-set error at matched coverage 0.6440.644 is 0.1430.143 on calib against 0.1270.127 on eval, so the held-out half is not harder. Under the isotonic ranking the same comparison reads 0.0920.092 against 0.1300.130, an in-sample optimism of 0.0510.051 on calib. The mechanism is that the calibrator and the threshold were fitted on the same 1,000 decisions, and isotonic’s in-sample fit sinks its own training errors below the gate. The one-parameter single-temperature calibrator, which cannot re-rank decisions within a primitive, lands at the target out of sample (τ=0.75\tau=0.75: calib 0.0940.094, eval 0.1000.100 at coverage 0.5980.598). A counterfactual rule that requires the 95% upper confidence bound on calib accepted error to clear the target picks τ=0.80\tau=0.80 under both a Wilson bound (0.0860.086) and a case-cluster bootstrap 95th percentile (0.0820.082), delivering 0.1010.101 at coverage 0.5340.534 on eval. The frozen point-estimate rule’s τ∗=0.70\tau^{*}=0.70 had a calib Wilson upper bound of 0.1160.116, already above the target it was meant to guarantee.

Case-level gating collapses.

At τcase∗=0.80\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{case}}=0.80, requiring all five decisions confident leaves coverage 0.0550.055 [0.025,0.085][0.025,0.085] (eleven accepted cases), with accepted-set accuracy 0.85450.8545 (error 0.1450.145, also missing target) and no significant advantage over random case escalation (E1t case variant: Δ=+0.005\Delta=+0.005, p=0.075p=0.075; secondary, outside the confirmatory family). The all-five-confident requirement is too conservative to be useful at these confidence levels; decision-level gating is the only viable mode measured here.

High-confidence errors in security and invoice decisions.

Among accepted decisions at τ∗=0.70\tau^{*}=0.70 on eval, security_incidents has 2626 errors in 177177 accepted decisions (14.7%14.7\%) and invoice_processing 16/18716/187 (8.6%8.6\%). The single most confident security error is instructive: case security_incidents_000043, severity (score), predicted 33 at calibrated confidence 1.01.0 against a unanimous teacher gold of 44 (label_agreement records no split, ruling out a teacher-ambiguity artifact). The top invoice errors are mostly teacher-split cases, ambiguous items the gate should have escalated. A cascade whose accepted set contains confidence-1.01.0 security misclassifications is not made safe by an 86%86\% average. Isotonic’s saturating upper knots (which map high raw confidence to exactly 1.01.0) make the top of the confidence scale uninformative, an argument for the temperature family on operational grounds even before A6’s statistical failure.

Cost and latency (E6).

Latency and throughput are the canonical E1 measurements of §4 (this hardware only; a step-8 re-measurement that ran concurrently with Track B training measured p50 204204 ms and is superseded as contended, Appendix C). Cascade cost per decision is cL+(1−c)​cTc_{L}+(1-c)\,c_{T} with measured cL≈18.4c_{L}\approx 18.4 ms/decision amortized (batch 1, 2,0002{,}000 decisions in 36.836.8 s) and cTc_{T} symbolic; at the frozen operating point the escalation term is 0.328​cT0.328\,c_{T}. Third-party cascade economics in adjacent settings appear in §2; no comparison to them is claimed.

8 Robustness (E7), ablations (E8), and the Track B replication

All E7 perturbations ran on calib cases only (no eval exposure; calib is itself half of the official test split, per the exposure ledger in §3.7); everything in this section is exploratory under the frozen plan except the Track B family rows (C/D/E2t), which are confirmatory. All numbers measured.

Option-order permutations.

Across four seeded permutations of every choice decision’s option order (300300 decisions ×\times 4 runs), 6.75%6.75\% of predictions flip; accuracy ranges 0.7270.727–0.7630.763 across runs against 0.7470.747 original. The predicted-position histogram is flat over positions 00–33 (287/291/243/293287/291/243/293) with position 4 at 8686, but position 4 exists only for k=5k=5 questions, so the small count reflects option-count composition rather than avoidance. This is far milder than the option-position pathologies documented for generative LLM judges (Zheng et al., 2024; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Wang et al., 2024); a typed encoder head appears structurally less order-sensitive, though 6.75%6.75\% of flips is not zero and would touch ∼20{\sim}20 decisions per 400-case batch.

Surface perturbations (substitute for paraphrase; deviation D2).

The planned paraphrase test named no runnable paraphraser, so two deterministic surface transforms substitute, and are labeled as such. Lowercasing with punctuation stripped flips 1.7%1.7\% of predictions (accuracy 0.772→0.7700.772\to 0.770); a neutral prefix flips 1.4%1.4\% (→0.777\to 0.777). Mean confidence shifts are <0.003{<}0.003. This tests format brittleness only, not semantic robustness; no paraphrase claim is made.

Missing evidence lowers confidence.

Dropping a load-bearing state field before re-scoring changes 4949–66%66\% of that workflow’s predictions and cuts its accuracy roughly in half (e.g. customer_service:thread: flip rate 0.6560.656, accuracy 0.800→0.3320.800\to 0.332; security_incidents:alert: 0.5080.508, →0.500\to 0.500; invoice_processing:invoice: 0.4920.492, →0.476\to 0.476; agent_trace_observability:trace_summary: 0.5720.572, →0.324\to 0.324). The assessor-relevant finding is the confidence direction. For every load-bearing field the mean confidence drops (e.g. −0.113-0.113 for thread, −0.058-0.058 for trace_summary), i.e. the model becomes less confident when evidence is missing, which is the gate behavior a cascade needs. Peripheral fields (orders, constraints) flip ≤5%{\leq}5\% with negligible shifts. Figure 7 shows all fields.

Label shift and option-count stress.

Importance-reweighting calib to a uniform gold-label distribution per (workflow, question) drops accuracy from 0.7720.772 to 0.6880.688; roughly 0.080.08 of headline accuracy rides on the benchmark’s skewed label priors. Synthetic single-question retrieval probes at k∈{5,10,20,30}k\in\{5,10,20,30\} options all score 100%100\% (4040 probes each; trivial by design, not comparable to benchmark accuracy). They confirm the only live site of the shipped choice:11+ clamp; at k≥11k\geq 11 the raw temperature 0.10060.1006 is clamped to 0.50.5, and mean probe confidence jumps to 0.970.97/0.940.94. The clamp region is exactly where the configuration sharpens most aggressively, on the least tested inputs.

Ablations (E8; stored eval records only, no new forwards).

The calibration ×\times cascade 2×22\times 2 shows the interaction that matters. Gating shipped confidences at τ=0.70\tau=0.70 accepts only 18.8%18.8\% of decisions (at 0.9950.995 accepted accuracy) because under-confident scores rarely clear the bar, while the calibrated pipeline accepts 67.2%67.2\% at 0.8600.860; calibration is what makes the gate’s coverage usable at all. Among confidence statistics at matched 67.2%67.2\% coverage, negative entropy edges out max-probability (0.86610.8661 vs. 0.86010.8601 accepted accuracy) and margin trails (0.85420.8542); ordinal variance on score decisions only is worst (0.82900.8290). Per primitive, isotonic repairs ECE15 from 0.238/0.193/0.1860.238/0.193/0.186 to 0.066/0.035/0.0630.066/0.035/0.063 (choice/noul/score) with accuracy essentially unchanged. The naive-vs-cluster interval contrast is case-cluster BCa width 0.0640.064 vs. naive i.i.d. 0.0540.054, ratio 1.1851.185 (Figure 8).

8.1 The Track B clean replication and the price of contamination

Track B retrains from the pinned laya base with the card’s RLCD recipe on case-level splits (960960 fine-tune / 240240 validation cases, seed 2026092620260926; one Apple-silicon device), then touches the 400-case test split exactly once with its own independently frozen pipeline (validation-fitted methods; winner again isotonic; τdec∗=0.75\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{dec}}=0.75). The identity configuration is the trained checkpoint’s own per-type temperatures, fitted on the 240 validation cases during training (1.1451.145, 1.1221.122, 1.1971.197 for choice, score, noul; run manifest), and methods (2)–(6) are fitted on top of it.

Replication. Test accuracy 0.77100.7710 [0.7495,0.7905][0.7495,0.7905] vs. the released checkpoint’s 0.76700.7670; paired case-level difference +0.0040+0.0040 [−0.009,+0.017][-0.009,+0.017], p=0.568p=0.568; the card’s training recipe replicates within noise under a cleaner protocol, on different hardware, with case-level splits. But the identity configurations differ sharply in probability quality. Track B’s validation-fitted temperatures give test NLL 0.62710.6271 vs. 0.70690.7069 and ECE15 0.15090.1509 vs. 0.21420.2142 (paired Δ\DeltaNLL −0.0798-0.0798 [−0.089,−0.070][-0.089,-0.070], Δ\DeltaECE −0.0634-0.0634 [−0.075,−0.048][-0.075,-0.048], both p≤2×10−4p\leq 2{\times}10^{-4}). Same recipe, same accuracy, but this cross-checkpoint contrast alone cannot isolate the cause; Track B also carries newly trained weights, a different optimization trajectory, and different hardware. The calibration-protocol attribution rests on the within-Track-B contamination probe below, which holds the weights fixed.

The selection-rule failure replicates. Track B’s frozen rule again picked isotonic (validation NLL 0.4890.489 vs. 0.5600.560 single-temperature), and again the held-out NLL contrast failed (C6: Δ=−0.046\Delta=-0.046 [−0.094,+0.012][-0.094,+0.012], p=0.108p=0.108) while every temperature-family contrast (C2–C5, D2–D6) rejected at p≤2×10−4p\leq 2{\times}10^{-4}. Track B’s cascade also repeats Track A’s pattern. The frozen τdec∗=0.75\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{dec}}=0.75 (validation accepted error 0.08660.0866) misses the target on test (0.10280.1028; coverage 0.58350.5835 [0.557,0.609][0.557,0.609], accepted accuracy 0.89720.8972 [0.876,0.914][0.876,0.914]), and beats random escalation decisively (E2t: Δ=+0.0757\Delta=+0.0757 [0.0661,0.0851][0.0661,0.0851], one-sided p≤10−4p\leq 10^{-4}). The two tracks, with independent fitting splits, recorded the same two qualitative failures, which places both in the frozen procedure at this sample size rather than in either split. The §7 decomposition holds in the same direction here (validation 0.0866→0.0866\to test 0.10280.1028; single-temperature gating on test reaches 0.1050.105 at τ=0.70\tau=0.70; deviation D9).

Contamination probe. Refitting per-primitive temperatures on 400400 decisions the model trained on (the released checkpoint’s own protocol, per the fine-tuning notebook linked from the model card) yields temperatures (0.400,0.309,0.219)(0.400,0.309,0.219) vs. the clean validation’s (0.582,0.541,0.638)(0.582,0.541,0.638); training-set confidence looks sharper than it is, so the fit sharpens beyond what held-out data supports. Held-out test ECE15 degrades from 0.02360.0236 (clean fit) to 0.08730.0873 (contaminated fit), a 3.7×3.7\times inflation at identical accuracy. This is an upper-bound probe (the notebook’s actual holdout was item-level within partially seen cases, between these regimes), but it measures the mechanism and its direction directly.

9 External validity (E9)

[DESCOPED: preregistration §0.a: no external-set results will be reported in this version. Conclusions are restricted to the synthetic benchmark.]

The pre-freeze experiment plan (not released; summarized in the preregistration’s §0.a) specified an external set of 120 independently sourced, human-adjudicated cases (two blinded annotators, third-adjudicator protocol, chance-corrected agreement reporting). The preregistration’s §0.a amendment records that no annotator pool exists for this version and exercises the plan’s stated fallback (its §3.3, option 3): state so “plainly” and restrict every conclusion to the synthetic benchmark (the word is the plan’s). We do that; no numbers from the planned external set exist, and the two external-validity members of the confirmatory family (F1t/F2t; hypothesis H4) are reported as not executed (Appendix E). What follows in §9.1 is a separate, post-registration exploratory probe and is no substitute for that set.

9.1 An exploratory out-of-distribution probe (E10)

Because the planned external set is descoped, we ran one post-registration exploratory probe of our own, labeled as such on every artifact and never entering the confirmatory family (H4 remains untested; F1t/F2t remain not executed). The probe asks whether the released checkpoint (F16 weights) transfers zero-shot to evidence-grounded claim verification over documents from its own four workflow domains. We authored a corpus of 24 fictional workflow documents (six per domain, 150–192 words each) and 120 typed claims about them, balanced 60 supported / 60 not-supported across six claim types (paraphrase, inference, number, entity, contradiction, unverifiable; 20 each), with verbatim evidence spans recorded for every verifiable claim and a validator script enforcing the corpus constraints. The harness is standard retrieval-augmented noul querying (sentence-aware ∼55{\sim}55-word chunks, MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, cosine top-k=5k{=}5, one yes/no question per claim through predict_batch), with document-level cluster bootstrap intervals. All measured, exploratory.

The checkpoint does not transfer. Accuracy is 0.6170.617 [0.533,0.683][0.533,0.683] (balanced accuracy the same), against 0.8580.858 (measured) on the benchmark’s own in-distribution noul decisions, a drop of roughly 0.240.24. The two noul tasks are related but not identical, so the delta is a directional signal rather than a like-for-like measurement. One in three unsupported claims is accepted (false acceptance 0.3330.333 [0.218,0.439][0.218,0.439]). Confidence barely ranks the errors: AUROC 0.5890.589 [0.495,0.683][0.495,0.683], and the confidence distribution compresses below ∼0.77{\sim}0.77, so the frozen gating rule is infeasible on this set. No grid threshold reaches the 0.100.10 error target at nonzero coverage, and coverage dies before error improves (at τ=0.65\tau=0.65: coverage 0.1750.175, accepted error still 0.2380.238). Per claim type, contradiction (0.7500.750) and number (0.7000.700) are detected best; entity swaps and one-step inference sit at chance (0.5000.500 each), the failures most dangerous for evidence checking. Retrieval is not the whole explanation (evidence recall@5 is 0.840.84).

On this probe’s evidence, the in-distribution results of §5–8 are properties of the benchmark match, and nothing in this paper licenses deploying this checkpoint as a claim verifier or on any distribution it was not fine-tuned for. This probe is our own design and instrumentation end to end (corpus, claims, validator, harness); its corpus, per-decision predictions, validation record, and results are in the ancillary files (anc/e10/).

10 Discussion

Benchmark circularity, and what 0.7670.767 can and cannot mean.

The measured accuracy (0.7670.767; measured) sits above the teacher’s own self-agreement ceiling (0.7350.735; reported) and well above the perfect-factor-knowledge reference (0.7040.704; reported). The dataset card’s own interpretation rule says scores much above ∼0.75{\sim}0.75 indicate a model has learned the teacher’s idiosyncrasies rather than the task. The correct reading of E1 is therefore that a 421M specialist fine-tuned on these four workflows saturates agreement with a noisy synthetic teacher on held-out cases from the same generator; no “beats the teacher” reading survives that ceiling. Teacher agreement is not correctness (Gudibande et al., 2023); a model can be penalized for being right where the teacher is wrong. This is also why no superiority claim over JEV is available from any table here. The third-party JEV row (0.7270.727; third-party) was produced by a different party under different prompts and pipeline on a benchmark whose ceiling is 0.7350.735. The specialist/generalist grouping makes the rows non-comparable by the dataset card’s own discipline. A zero-shot hosted model on the same card also clears the ceiling (0.7680.768; third-party), so the ceiling is a reading rule for a specialist fitted to this teacher rather than a hard cap on any model; the claim here concerns only what the specialist’s score can mean.

Direction of miscalibration is an operational quantity.

Two checkpoints with ECE 0.210.21 can fail in opposite directions. An over-confident assessor silently passes errors through a cascade gate, while an under-confident one escalates too much and erodes the cost case. The shipped Laya artifact is the second kind (§4.2), with the mechanism measured in §6. After proper calibration the signed gap flips to slightly positive (+0.028+0.028 for the single temperature and +0.033+0.033 for the selected isotonic map on eval), mild over-confidence, which is the regime in which the E5 gate under-delivers. Direction of miscalibration, not its magnitude, determines which cascade failure mode a deployment gets, and the threshold was chosen on the calibrator’s own fitting data, so its in-sample accepted-set error understated the held-out error (the §7 decomposition).

Procedure-level failures the preregistration recorded.

One frozen design choice produced both recorded failures. The calibrator and the threshold were fitted on the same split, under an NLL-based selection rule that favors expressive calibrators, so the selected isotonic map overfit (A6/C6). The same in-sample optimism let τ∗\tau^{*} clear a target it could not hold out of sample (H3a; decomposition in §7). Without preregistration both would have been silently “fixed” (swap in the vector method, nudge τ\tau to 0.750.75) and the paper would have reported only successes. The recorded failures measure the generalization gap of the procedure, which is what a practitioner reusing this recipe on their own 200-case calibration set needs to know (Nosek et al., 2018). The reusable lesson is to cross-fit (fit the calibrator on one half of the fitting split, choose τ\tau on the other) or to select τ\tau by an upper confidence bound on the fitting-split error.

Where a compact typed assessor is the right tool.

The measured operating point, ∼19{\sim}19 ms per decision at batch 1 on a laptop-class accelerator with full distribution outputs (measured; §4), is the argument for the interface. It is local, auditable, and cheap enough to run on every decision, with typed label spaces fixed by the workflow. Published cascades in adjacent settings (Li et al., 2026; Gisserot-Boukhlef et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024; Jitkrittum et al., 2023) suggest such a first stage can carry most of a workload when its confidence orders its errors, and that thresholds must be validated locally. This study now has the measured version of that advice. The confidence signal beat random escalation at matched rate on both tracks, and calibration is what made the gate’s coverage usable at all (E8). In-distribution, the measured posture is that a compact typed assessor plus one fitted temperature is a useful triage stage at roughly two-thirds coverage. That holds provided the error target is treated as an estimate to monitor, not a guarantee, and the accepted set is audited (§7). Out of distribution, the exploratory probe measured no transfer (§9.1); nothing in this paper counters that.

11 Limitations

  1. 1.

    Single checkpoint, single configuration. One released artifact at one pinned revision, as shipped; no model-family sweep, no seed variation.

  2. 2.

    Synthetic, teacher-labeled benchmark. Gold is the mean of three samples from one ∼{\sim}4B-class teacher; every metric is agreement with that teacher rather than correctness (Gudibande et al., 2023); cases are template-generated, with no fielded deployment behind them.

  3. 3.

    No compute-matched architectural comparison. Comparators differ in size, training exposure, and interface; grouping by task access mitigates but does not remove this.

  4. 4.

    No TypeSafe JEV access. All JEV figures are third-party on different pipelines and samples; nothing here supports a head-to-head ranking in either direction.

  5. 5.

    No preregistered external validity set in this version (descoped; §9); every confirmatory conclusion is restricted to the synthetic benchmark, and H4 goes untested. The E10 probe (§9.1) is exploratory, post-registration, self-authored (120 claims, 24 documents), and its claims are correspondingly weak, a transfer-failure signal rather than a measurement of external validity.

  6. 6.

    No independent annotator pool. The external-set annotation protocol (two blinded annotators, adjudication, agreement statistics) exists only in the unreleased pre-freeze plan; no human adjudication of any model output occurred in this version.

  7. 7.

    Single hardware configuration. Apple M5 Max / MPS; latency and throughput are not comparable to the card’s T4 numbers or to any served deployment, and the observed non-monotonic batching behavior is unexplained.

  8. 8.

    Track A’s fitting data is structurally contaminated. The released checkpoint saw all 1,200 training cases, so Track A’s calib is carved from the test split as mitigation; only Track B is clean end-to-end.

  9. 9.

    Small fitting and evaluation splits. Track A fits on 200 cases and evaluates on 200; both replicated frozen-procedure failures (isotonic selection, τ∗\tau^{*} transfer) are properties at this sample size and may vanish with more fitting data. Conversely, the τ\tau miss means the study cannot certify any error target at n=200n=200, and the exploratory decomposition in §7 traces that miss to in-sample optimism of the same-split fit (deviation D9).

  10. 10.

    Soft accuracy did not reproduce. It measures 0.5090.509 against a reported 0.4710.471 with a CI excluding the reported value; an fp32/CPU rerun rules out precision and backend (deviation D10), a version bisection rules out every released harness version from 0.3.3 to 0.3.20 (deviation D11), and what remains, the card-side evaluation pipeline or data state, is not recoverable from the card (§4).

  11. 11.

    The ModernBERT-base comparator uses a different recipe from the card’s row. Our RLCD-trained specialist measures 0.54250.5425 against the dataset card’s frozen-encoder Adaptive-Classifier specialist at 0.6460.646; the training methods differ, so the row is a recipe comparison, not a reproduction of the card’s experiment (§5).

  12. 12.

    Shipped confidence carries a known configuration defect (a training-slice temperature fit, reported on the model card, overridden by an inherited table whose out-of-range entry laya 0.3.20 clamps; measured), the card says to treat it as uncalibrated, and choice-primitive ECE (0.2550.255) is worse than the aggregate (0.2140.214); the headline calibration number flatters the weakest primitive.

  13. 13.

    E1 predates the preregistration (exempt because it fits nothing), so H1’s numerical criterion is a post-hoc reporting structure, and the E1-derived under-confidence observation informed the framing of the frozen E4 questions.

  14. 14.

    The paraphrase test was substituted (deviation D2); the surface transforms that ran test format brittleness only, and semantic paraphrase robustness is unmeasured.

  15. 15.

    E7’s option-count probes are synthetic retrieval tasks, trivial by construction; they locate where the shipped clamp is live but say nothing about accuracy at high option counts on real questions.

  16. 16.

    Latency/throughput are single-machine numbers. One planned re-measurement was invalidated by resource contention with concurrent training and is superseded by the uncontended E1 measurement (Appendix C).

12 Ethics and responsible use

The four workflows include payment release and security containment. Nothing in this paper supports using this checkpoint, or any assessor, as the sole arbiter of such decisions. The confidence signal is measurably miscalibrated as shipped, the calibrated cascade still missed its frozen error target on both tracks, and the accepted set contained high-confidence security errors (§7). The defensible deployment posture remains decision support with human accountability, thresholds validated locally on the deployment’s own distribution, and periodic re-checks. The benchmark is synthetic (no personal data, no human subjects); the planned external-set collection, when it happens, will carry its own annotation-ethics protocol. The dataset is Apache-2.0; model and code artifacts are used under their published terms; no credentials or account metadata appear in the released artifacts.

13 Independence statement

The author has no affiliation with, funding from, or financial interest in Convai Innovations (publisher of the model, its base model, and the laya package), the LocalLLaMA Hugging Face organization (publisher of the benchmark), or TypeSafe. E1 is an independent reproduction. The study’s integrity measures are: the analysis plan was frozen before any fitting touched the test split (§3.7); the acceptance gate’s one timing failure is disclosed in gate.json; results unfavorable and favorable to the artifact are reported with the same prominence; per-decision artifacts for every headline run are released so any party can recompute every number.

The E6 latency run executed while Track B training occupied the same accelerator (p50 204204 ms vs. 95.995.9 ms uncontended); it is retained in the artifact but superseded in the paper by the canonical, uncontended E1 measurement, labeled as such (§7).

  6. 6.

    D5: post-registration exploratory experiment added (E10). The out-of-distribution claim-verification probe of §9.1 was designed and run after the freeze. It touches no benchmark split, enters no confirmatory test, and is labeled exploratory on every artifact; it is logged here because it is a post-registration addition to the study’s scope.

  7. 7.

    D6: correction of a frozen misstatement (Brier target convention). The frozen plan (§8) attributed the card’s 0.0620.062 Brier to the one-hot form; verification against the code of the fine-tuning notebook linked from the model card shows it is the vs-teacher form (one-hot measures ≈0.37{\approx}0.37, vs-teacher 0.06580.0658). The paper reports the correct convention (Table 1); no measured value, selection, or test changes; the frozen document is not edited, and this entry is the correction of record.

  8. 8.

    D7: card-ECE bin-convention reconciliation. The preregistration froze the card-comparability ECE at 10 bins; manuscript drafts (and one artifact key, ece_card_M15) described it as 15 bins. The paper now uses the frozen 10-bin definition for “card convention” and labels equal-width M=15M{=}15 as the frozen confirmatory endpoint. Numerically invisible on E1; uniform under-confidence collapses every binned variant to 0.214230.21423 (§4.2); no confirmatory test is affected (the family was always defined on equal-width M=15M{=}15).

  9. 9.

    D8: p-value convention correction. The preregistration (§9) froze the raw tail-fraction formula p=2​min⁡(P⁡(Δ∗≤0),P⁡(Δ∗≥0))p=2\min(P(\Delta^{*}\leq 0),P(\Delta^{*}\geq 0)) (one-sided where specified), which encodes zero exceedances in 10,00010{,}000 resamples as p=0p=0. At round-1 review this was replaced by the finite-sample add-one convention (b+1)/(B+1)(b{+}1)/(B{+}1), doubled for two-sided tests (§3.6). fdr_family_v2.json stores the corrected values with the raw tail fractions preserved per row (p_raw); the original fdr_family.json is retained unchanged; BH recomputed from the corrected p-values changes no decision (20 of 22 executed tests reject; A6 and C6 still fail).

  10. 10.

    D9: post-hoc decomposition of the τ∗\tau^{*} miss (2026-09-27). An exploratory analysis added at external review, released as e11_tau_decomposition.json, recomputes accepted-set error at matched coverage under the identity and isotonic rankings, sweeps the frozen τ\tau grid under the single-temperature calibrator, and evaluates a counterfactual upper-confidence-bound selection rule. Inputs are stored records and grid rows only, all in the ancillary files; no model forwards ran, and Track B’s validation side uses stored grid-row aggregates (its per-decision records were produced afterwards; D10). No frozen number, verdict, threshold, or table changes; the analysis is labeled exploratory and post hoc where it appears (§7).

  11. 11.

    D10: fp32/CPU probe and Track B validation records (2026-09-27). Two additions at external review, neither changing a frozen number. (i) An exploratory fp32/CPU rerun of the 2,000 E1 decisions (e1_fp32_cpu_probe.json plus a per-decision file; canonical E1 artifacts untouched) reproduces the canonical run, F16 weights under bf16 autocast on MPS (soft accuracy 0.50870.5087 vs. 0.50860.5086; max probability difference 0.00790.0079; 4 argmax flips), ruling out precision and backend (§4). A planned second leg on hosted T4 hardware could not be run from this environment. (ii) Track B validation per-decision records (track_b_validation_decisions.json), from a forward pass on the 240 validation cases only with the frozen calibration parameters reapplied; a sanity gate confirmed the winner’s records reproduce the stored τ∗\tau^{*} grid row exactly (n=704n=704, accepted error 0.08660.0866), and the test set was not touched. These records postdate the D9 analysis.

  12. 12.

    D11: laya version bisection of the soft-accuracy discrepancy (2026-09-27). Exploratory reruns of the 2,000 E1 decisions in one fresh virtual environment per laya release, on the canonical backend (MPS) with torch 2.14.0 and transformers 5.17.0 pinned, so only the harness version varies (artifacts e1_version_probe_*.json with per-decision files and one manifest per run; canonical artifacts untouched; fits nothing). Release 0.3.20 reproduces the canonical run with maximum probability difference 0.00.0 at the stored rounding; release 0.3.3 (single-state predict API, run through a batch-of-one adapter after the first attempt failed on the missing predict_batch method, manifested) measures soft accuracy 0.50870.5087 with 4 argmax flips (it differs from the canonical run on the same 1,923 decisions as the fp32/CPU probe, with the same four flips and the same maximum probability difference of 0.00790.0079; 1,910 of the 1,923 difference vectors are digit-identical at the files’ stored precision, consistent with 0.3.3 running without autocast). The endpoints agree, so per the pre-stated rule no intermediate release was run; the released 0.3.3–0.3.20 harness range is ruled out as the cause (§4).

One provenance note: track_b_split.json was written by the training driver about two minutes after the training manifest opened; the split is deterministic from seed 20260926 and its contents match the preregistration’s description.

The third-party out-of-distribution report the preregistration anticipated citing is omitted from this version; §9.1 stands on the exploratory probe alone.

Appendix E Confirmatory test family

The frozen family (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q=0.05q=0.05; 24 tests): A2–A6 and B2–B6: Track A eval paired differences in NLL and in equal-width M=15M{=}15 ECE for each calibration method versus identity (two-sided). C2–C6 and D2–D6: the same on Track B’s test run. E1t/E2t: oracle-scored cascade accuracy versus oracle-scored random escalation at matched rate on Track A eval and Track B respectively (one-sided). F1t/F2t: external-versus-in-distribution differences in accuracy and ECE (two-sided; not executed in this version, external set descoped, §9; conservatively kept in the BH denominator, m=24m=24). All other analyses are exploratory and are labeled as such wherever they appear. Table 5 gives every executed outcome (all measured); 20 of 22 executed tests reject. P-values carry the add-one correction of §3.6; fdr_family_v2.json stores the corrected values with raw tail fractions preserved per row, and recomputing BH from them changes no decision (the original fdr_family.json is retained unchanged).
